subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, September 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. McDermid that Bill C-73, an act to provide for the dissolution or transfer of certain Crown corporations and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if this were an isolated measure before us today, namely the proposal in the bill to dissolve, transfer or sell Canada Harbour Place, Canada Museums Construction Corporation, the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, the Canadian Patents and Development Limited, the Harbourfront Corporation and Mingan Associates Limited, this bill in its entirety and scope would be a source of concern.
This measure has to be seen against the background of a trend, a pattern. If we look at the record of the Conservative government on the matter of privatization, which actually is a very fancy word to replace the words dismantling Canada, and the interest of the Canadian public in a number of very fine initiatives, then we find a remarkably long list of measures that this government has carried out.
I would like to remind people of the sale of shares of Air Canada, the sale of the CN Hotels, the sale of a CN subsidiary called CN Route, and the sale of Canadair Limited. If that were not enough, this government
managed also to privatize Canadian Arsenals Limited and went on happily with the sale of de Havilland. Northern Canada Power Commission was not spared nor the Northern Transportation Company. Then there is Northwestel Inc., Pecheries Canada Inc., and in 1987 there was the sale of Teleglobe Canada, with proceeds of some $500 million in cash from that sale, a crucial and key industry. There is Terra Nova Telecommunications Inc. on the list of corporations that have been partially or entirely sold.
Crown holdings that have been sold include CNCP, and probably the jewel in the Crown in the sixties and seventies when we were attempting, and were quite successful, to establish Canadian public ownership in key industries, the Canada Development Corporation. Add to that Fishery Products International Limited, Nanisivik Mines Ltd., and Varity Corporation.
To that, one must add initiatives which are now being considered. What emerges is a picture of the Government of Canada under Tory stewardship busily intent on dismantling public ownership in this country.
In doing so, whenever there is the sale of an item, we do not always know whether the new owners will be Canadians or foreign interests, thus increasing of course ownership on the part of foreign investors.
This is a very disturbing pattern, but we cannot accuse the Tories of being inconsistent. Actually, the Progressive Conservative Party has been very consistent in this matter. It has promised to privatize Canada, and it is doing that quite effectively. It is giving away the public interest to the private sector, and sometimes to the private foreign sector.
That is a very disturbing fact, which nobody in this House can deny. In addition to that, we have seen the dissolution of the Foreign Investment Review Agency in 1985. We have seen a constant systematic weakening of the CBC. We are now at the eve of the sale of Petro-Canada about which many of us will be denied the right to speak because of closure.

I would like to remind you, Madam Speaker, that when Petro-Canada was introduced in the seventies, as the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands quite rightly pointed out the other day, closure was introduced after 15 days of debate. This government allowed debate for only two days before introducing closure, thus denying probably half of all membership in this House an opportunity to speak.
We are on the eve of the sale of Petro-Canada, which is the wrong thing to do for a number of reasons, which would take all the time allotted for this intervention. Madam Speaker, you have the privatizing of Unemployment Insurance through Bill C-21, because the public interest has been withdrawn in the funding of that very important commission. Madam Speaker, there is also the partial privatization of Air Canada.
At this rate, Madam Speaker, the day will come when this government, if given the chance to continue to govern, will attempt possibly to privatize Parliament Hill. It will try to find a good American sponsor, someone probably like Coca-Cola, Kodak or as my colleague from York South says, perhaps McDonald's or Kentucky Fried Chicken? Why not? It could be a very profitable place to privatize. Madam Speaker, you could make money. Why not let this public investment go into the hands of the private sector and into the hands of these great entrepreneurs who know how to make a profit?
Why does the minister in charge of privatization not make a proposal in this House for the privatization of old age pensions? They could also be privatized. Why not? It is a very legitimate way of making money.
The government is already privatizing the airports in Toronto, are they not? It is an interesting theme. There is a phenomenal investment in the name of the public which, the moment it could become profitable-business enterprise in the hands of the public sector can be profitable as well as when it is in private hands. There is no reason why the Canadian public cannot reap the benefits of good management and still retain ownership.
Nowhere in any text of economics has it been disclaimed, Madam Speaker, that you can have the Canadian public as a winner maintaining and retaining its
ownership rather than transforming public ownership into some kind of supermarket and allowing the latest arrival on the market to make money at the expense and with the benefit of the Canadian public.
That is Tory theology. In that sense, we can only say that they are being consistent. Why not privatize the Bank of Canada? The pattern is there. Perhaps tomorrow, we will see a proposal to that effect. If it could be profitable, the government would not stop at proposing to privatize Parliament Hill. It would also privatize the Canadian army, but there it would have some difficulties because nowhere, yet, in recent times, has a government been able to privatize its army successfully.
Bill C-73 has to be seen against that background. It is not just an isolated initiative. It is not just something that happened all of a sudden around the cabinet table because the minister wanted to make a mark in history by coming to the House to pass a bill and demonstrate that he is active. This is part and parcel, consistent with Tory ideology: the dismantling of public ownership in Canada. Of course, in the next election we will make sure that this fact is not forgotten by the electorate.
Moving to the measure itself, Madam Speaker, because time is short, let us examine what the minister promises, what is in the bill, and what the Crombie royal commission recommends.
The minister in his intervention in the House assured the nation that when it comes to the sale of the Toronto Harbourfront Corporation, which he wants to wind up and dissolve, that the following will take place, and I am reading from Hansard at page 13555:

Suddenly, we are saying: "Well, let's sell it. Harbourfront can go. Give up your lake and say goodbye".
That leads me to this excellent report, The Water Shed by the former member for Rosedale. He was a very fine minister while he was here in Ottawa and probably left because he was utterly frustrated. On page 129 of that report, under the heading "The Future of Harbourfront", the Royal Commission on the Future of the Toronto Waterfront states: "The lands, properties, and residual interests now managed by Harbourfront Corporation and those still in the inventory of Public Works Canada should be held and administered by Public Works Canada, on a temporary basis, until appropriate agreements with the city are implemented." That is not in Bill C-73 and it is very legitimate for the Opposition to raise this at this point and to ask why it is not in Bill C-73.
In making recommendations regarding the future of the Toronto waterfront in another report, the same author, Mr. Crombie, stated, and I quote from Parks, Pleasures and Public Amenities, volume 4, at page 68: "We recommend first that there be no further sale of lands currently held in public ownership." How do you like that?
Where is the co-ordination, the integration, the synchronisation between the government and its own Royal Commission? Maybe someone from the government benches will rise to offer an answer, a justification, or some kind of an explanation.
What is the point of having the Royal Commission on the Future of the Toronto Waterfront produce this outstanding documentation and give recommendations, only to have a silly little bill, Bill C-73, ignoring the work that has gone on for the protection of one of the most important waterfronts in Canada? It does not make sense. It is insane.
Time does not permit me to analyse what is being proposed in Vancouver. Again, another beautiful, private grab is shaping up in that city as well. I will stick to my own home city.
It is quite clear that this bill, Bill C-73, is reflective of the Tory vision. It is a vision which uses the public and what is in public ownership for the promotion of the interests of large business and powerful interests in society. Not only that, but it offers the opportunity to the private interests in society, utilizing investments originally made with public funds. First, the public is asked to take the risk. Madam Speaker, there is nothing so revisionist as the Liberal mentality. Huang Danczkay got the site on which to build the shoddiest apartment buildings that were ever built at the time because of the rules imposed on the Harbourfront Corporation by the Liberal cabinet of the day. The city of Toronto was left no choice by the cabinet of the day if it wanted to have access for public use of the public park but that that project be approved. Those were the rules of the Harbourfront Corporation imposed by the Liberal cabinet of the day that many of us tried to stop.
The hon. member chooses to drag my family's name into it. Yes, my family is in the real estate business. We were also the longest serving directors of the Toronto Harbour Commission, and my grandfather was also the chairman for the longest number of years of anybody. I can tell the hon. member that not once in our professional lives did we take a fee or have anything to do with anything in the harbourfront for 14 years because we value it. One of the reasons I became involved in municipal politics was to try and stop what Liberals were then doing to my harbour.
For the member to suggest now that the destruction of the Harbourfront property was caused by anything other than the rules that were imposed by the Liberal cabinet is so revisionist it is beyond the pale. What we needed then and what we need now is the greatest possible local control of that site by local entity, however the players involved choose to negotiate the end product that will come out of those negotiations. I do not know whether it will be new a Crown corporation that is provincial or a new Crown corporation that is local. I do not know what it will be. It will be whatever the partners who are all government partners choose it to be. That is what this is designed to allow to happen.
I suppose I should not be surprised, but for Liberals who created this mess to ignore the heritage they created and say that somehow this is an attempt to turn it over to the private developers is unbelievable.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, I want to say that I am not one who is opposed to privatization in certain conditions. I am not one who is opposed to looking at Crown corporations and seeing if they have outlived their public purpose. If all of a sudden the private sector wants to get involved because it can do a better job, I have absolutely no problem with that.
I am also one, by the way, who is not running away from Harbourfront. I happen to believe that Harbour-front is a multicultural mecca. Sure, it has some flaws, but I think it is one of the finest people places in North America.
I think of many of the joint ventures between the Government of Canada and the private sector, such as the Queen's Quay, the first building that went up with Olympia and York. It was a great joint venture. During the special recovery program period during 1981-82, when times were so bad, we were able to add parking lots. We have a great antique market down there and a beautiful skating rink that people use during the winter. All of these are pluses.
Even though the processing of the apartments on Harbourfront is really questionable, I happen to think that Huang Danczkay who built these apartments in record time, with all of the problems, probably did not do a bad job. There were many great builders and developers that pulled Harbourfront up from absolutely no-
Govemment Orders
where and, in joint venture with the Government of Canada, made it one of the best people places in Canada with cultural and recreational events. The men and women who put it together over many years-Liberals, Tbries, NDP-helped to make it a great place.
Where my problem comes in with this bill is that Harbourfront, as it is evolving right now, is doing a fabulous job. We cannot ignore the fact that the Government of Canada, with taxpayers' money to the tune of about $250 million that has been put into this place, is part of the reason it is so great.
Now all of a sudden we come along and we have Harbourfront running beautifully. We have people sensitized to the fact that there should be no more development down there. Even though sometimes we think that green space is the only way to make a people place, we can also have development and density. That can also create a people park. I am satisfied with that.
What I cannot understand is why this government is taking a jewel like this, our Harbourfront, putting a book value of $31 million on it, and putting it up for grabs. I am really trying hard to understand the point of the hon. member for Don Valley West, although I resent the fact that he calls me some kind of a rat packer, because that is not my traditional style. I am not taking anything away from my colleagues, because there are different styles.
However, it is absolute craziness to take a public piece of property that is probably worth $300 million and put a book value on it of $31 million. If they were to say that they were going to transfer it to the public sector specifically, because maybe the city or the province could do a better job, then I would not have as much of a problem with it. I am a centralist, and I think that the national government should have some say in what goes on there. It is not just for the people of Toronto; it is also for tourism and people who come to our city.
I have a very serious concern about this Harbourfront deal. The developers who put Harbourfront together, not taking anything away from their craftsmanship, are great people; but it is the same group that is basically now in charge of, owning and running Terminal 3. When I say "owning", I know there is a technical word here called a "lease". It is a 40-year lease with a 20-year option on the third largest airport in North America.

What concerns me is that this bill is so tricky, because we have wrap-ups of museums, constructions, corporations, and the Patent Act. In there is also the harbour lands of B.C. I am absolutely dismayed that the Minister of Justice is supporting this bill.
Pearson International last year made $70 million profit. That is before depreciation, and a lot of people say that it is being run poorly; in other words, that the private sector could come in and do a better job and increase the value. I give you that, Madam Speaker. Maybe the private sector could come in and do a better job.
It has been over 10 years. That is $1 billion worth of profit that the Government of Canada has traditionally used to help make sure the tarmac surfaces were maintained and make sure that smaller airports were maintained around this country.
Now what has the Government of Canada done? The Government of Canada has given to the private sector Terminal 3, which is really nothing more than a cash box for the private sector. Yes, it will pay a certain amount each year under the terms of the lease. I cannot get that lease from the Minister of Justice. I cannot get my hands on it. Nobody has seen it, and that is one of the problems that we have in this government.
If it is such a good deal for the taxpayer, why not put it on the table? Why not show that it is such a good deal. I have no problems if in fact the taxpayer is properly being served here. Then so be it. Let it be privatized. However, I have been told by experts who are assisting in that airport project that basically it is a private sector operation and that the Government of Canada has no control on how the public is being served. The public benefit could really go out the window here.
This is one of the reasons I have concern about the Harbourfront in Tbronto. If we allow our Harbourfront to be in the hands of the private sector completely, with no government authority, and if we give away our national airport-not just Terminal 3, as the Minister of Transport announced the other day-what will happen? This is not an optional use facility. This is a facility the public must use. I do not mind if it is an optional facility that the private sector can run better. That is fine, but
this is not an optional use facility. It is a facility that the public has to use, and it is 50 per cent of the nation.

Madam Speaker, today I wish to pay tribute to a great resident of Montreal North, Dr. Jules Brodeur, who was awarded the Prix de la Recherche en sante et en securite du travail by the Institute of the same name. subtopic: HERITAGE LANGUAGES
HERITAGE LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the federal government's decision to seriously reduce support for the heritage languages program last spring has badly hurt the operation of many heritage language schools across Canada. Every child in a heritage language program is now feeling the effect of those cutbacks.
The establishment of a multimillion Heritage Languages Institute will in no way make up for the withdrawal of these basic life line funds for these schools. A non-partisan rally for heritage languages will be held on Parliament Hill at noon tomorrow, sponsored by the heritage language schools of eastern Ontario. A similar demonstration will be held at the same time in Saskatoon.
October 26, 1990

Across Canada heritage language schools are struggling to keep classes operating and to share their knowledge, languages and cultures with all Canadians. Heritage language programs are an investment in a global future for all Canadians.
All members of Parliament are urged to show their support and attend the rally for heritage languages on Parliament Hill at noon tomorrow.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this very moment, during Small Business Week 1990, Canadian entrepreneurs are facing a series of complex challenges. All those interested in the small business sector will have to pool their expertise, experience and foresight to gain an understanding of what we can expect in the years to come.
Madam Speaker, international markets, international competition and increasingly demanding consumers merely accentuate the problems facing small business.
With this in mind, in 1984 our government introduced its economic renewal program. As a result, we have made tremendous progress in creating new job opportunities, thanks to tax reform, deregulation and the abolition of trade barriers. The government's, challenge in the years to come will be to continue economic renewal, and businesses will have to adjust, to take advantage of the many new opportunities that will be available.

subtopic: DAVID IRVING
DAVID IRVING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, David Irving is speaking across Canada and will be in Ottawa at the Ottawa Congress Centre next month. He is spreading a message that the holocaust was a fabrication.
David Irving testified on behalf of Ernst Zundel that Nazi Germany had no official policy on the extermination of Jews and he doubted six million Jews were systematically killed.
Such holocaust denial is offensive to all Jews and to anyone who supports fundamental human rights and is bound to engender hostility towards some Canadians. Therefore, I especially question the appropriateness of providing Mr. Irving with a platform in a building owned by the government and operated at public expense.
I do not know whether Mr. Irving is a racist, but in my estimation he is certainly not an historian, and does not deserve our attention, but instead our condemnation.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Small Business Week recognizes and encourages the entrepreneurial spirit of thousands of Canadians who operate a small business in our country. This year's theme, Quality and Productivity: The Competitive Edge is most appropriate.
Small businesses are the cornerstone of the Canadian economy. They are the main source of new ideas and new wealth, and account for three-quarters of the jobs created in Canada in the past few years.
Small Business Week is highlighted by such activities as trade fairs, exhibitions, information sessions, conferences and award presentations in every region of Canada.
I will be attending an award presentation in my riding of St. Albert on October 27. The Chamber of Commerce will be presenting an award to the St. Albert businessman of the year. I am proud to recognize the men and women who, through their small businesses, contribute so much to the nation's prosperity.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the sun sets on Small Business Week, the darkness is closing on small business in Canada. High interest rates, free trade and the GST are all succeeding in driving more and more entrepreneurs out of business.

October 26, 1990
As we see a growing number of businesses go into receivership or bankruptcy, we have to ask ourselves where we will find the entrepreneurial spirit the government has talked about.
Will we find it in the small one and two-person firms whose operators do not have the will to continue in the face of becoming unpaid GST tax collectors for the federal government?
Will we find it in the furniture manufacturers who have gone broke?
Will we find it in the retailers along the U.S. border who are closing their shops because they can no longer compete with the Americans?
Will we find it in the hospitality industry which is already overburdened with taxation by this greedy government?
I strongly fear that the only spirit will be the ghost of small business, small business which has been killed by this government's policies.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, potato farmers in New Brunswick are facing a disaster. Heavy rains and wet weather this fall have placed this $70 million industry in jeopardy. As thousands of acres of potatoes lie rotting in the ground, as much as one-quarter of the crop is already lost.
The New Brunswick potato agency estimates that 20 per cent of those involved in the industry in my riding will be unable to survive this severe economic blow. At this time, we do not know what the cumulative loss will be, but we do know with certainty that difficulties lie ahead. We will be looking for a joint effort between the federal and provincial governments to assist.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS
INDIAN AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in an agreement reached between the province of Ontario and the federal government, the province recently announced that it will provide reserve land at no cost to the federal government for the six Ontario bands who have been fighting for reserve status since 1985.
The announcement is good news for the six bands, since they have been living in conditions not unlike those found in Third World countries. There is no running water, no indoor plumbing, no schools in some cases, no electricity, no telephone service and the housing is well below standard.
The only thing separating these communities from improved living conditions is the final approval by the federal cabinet. Cabinet approval of the agreement will provide the funding necessary to provide the residents of Kee-way-win, Wawakapewin, Saugeen, New Slate Falls, McDowell Lake and Aroland with the infrastructure they so desperately need.
Madam Speaker, I call on the Minister of Indian Affairs to press full steam ahead in order to ensure that cabinet approval is given by the end of the year. The government has to live up to the commitment it made on September 25 if it wants to demonstrate some good faith.

BILL C-43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Justice has said over and over again that a federal abortion law is needed to "occupy the field", to ensure that the provinces do not pass their own abortion laws.
Well, 17 of 18 constitutional experts disagreed. The New Democratic Party and the majority of the witnesses before the legislative committee on Bill C-43 disagreed. Now, the Nova Scotia courts have also told her she is wrong.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to offer my support to the comprehensive five-year plan for Canada's immigration policy announced yesterday.
In the tragic circumstances of poverty and homelessness for millions of people which we witness in so many places in the world today, surely our intentions to moderately increase our annual immigration levels by 50,000, a 20 per cent increase over five years, will be generously received and supported by all Canadians.
While Canada is noted for its humanitarian principles, there is also a basic demographic reality which immigration serves in this country, the sustaining of our own population levels so essential to our economic viability as a nation. Some experts advise that we should be taking in 1 per cent of our population each year just to keep our total population constant.
The new five-year plan, even with the increases, falls short of that minimum goal. Immigration is part of the challenge for a national commitment to multicultural-ism. Together those qualities help to make Canada a richer nation in all respects.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, here we are, at the eve of the second world climate conference in Geneva, and Canada has no position on carbon dioxide pollution reduction. Other countries have, but not Canada.
Why is the Minister of the Environment so reluctant? Is he afraid to give leadership? Is cabinet undecided because it is divided? Who pulls the strings? Is it the minister of energy, who believes that oil companies are philanthropists, operating in the public interest? While he fiddles, other nations are taking firm positions on cutting carbon dioxide pollution.
We are not giving leadership to the global community. No longer are our international positions, from Iraq to carbon dioxide pollution finalized in Ottawa. Alas, Madam Speaker, the Tory government takes its cues from the White House.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this past week more and more Canadians are applauding the long-awaited passage of Bill C-21, the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
These much-needed amendments improve the program's ability to help Canadian workers adjust to change.
Madam Speaker, the Canadian public increasingly appreciates the need for a well-trained workforce. They realize the need for a new attitude and approach to labour force training. Our workers deserve a national training effort which better meets the demands posed by structural and technological advancements.
Under Bill C-21, the commitment of an additional $800 million to training is another step in the right direction. To all Canadians I believe that it reflects our pursuit of an effective national training effort, as well as our commitment to helping Canadians find and keep jobs.

subtopic: THE ENVIRONMENT
THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, remember away back when the Prime Minister announced that a centre for sustainable development was to be opened in Winnipeg with a grant of $85 million dollars?
It all sounded so promising, the nation with the highest per capita energy use was going to do something of value. But somewhere along the way the wheels fell off. Funding for the centre turned out to be only $5 million and, as a constituent stated in a letter to me, the original proposal was reduced to tokenism and the concern with the environment tagged as rhetoric. As if that was not bad enough, the government announced a grant of $88 million toward construction of an opera house in Toronto, which makes you wonder about this government's priorities.

October 26, 1990
Oral Questions
I will give the last word to my constituent, who said in his letter to me: "Surely if money is available for a house of pleasure, then it should be available for a research centre that can help solve some of the world's environmental problems".

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES
PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was most pleased to hear of the imminent closure of the Kingston Penitentiary for Women. I would like to acknowledge the Solicitor General's diligence in this area and express gratitude on behalf of the women prisoners and their families.
I am sure that we can all empathize with the extra pain suffered by these women and their families as a result of this separation.
The creation of five new facilities for federally sentenced women located across the country is a humanitarian measure that is long overdue. While the changes came too late for some, who saw no way out of the situation but suicide, there is new hope for others. I am hoping that when the minister makes his decision on the locations of the facilities, that he takes Saskatchewan into consideration. Saskatchewan is centrally located within the prairie provinces.
The economic boost created by the construction, upkeep and employment of this facility would be greatly appreciated. More importantly, the need to keep a reasonable proximity between the women and their families is of paramount interest to the citizens of my home province.

subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS
HUMAN RIGHTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Italian Canadians, Chinese Canadians and Ukrainian Canadians are getting very tired of waiting for the Prime Minister to apologize for injustices that were perpetrated on innocent victims earlier in this century. This is important to our history.
Since 1983, we have been calling on the government to acknowledge the unjust Chinese head tax and Chinese Exclusion Act, which was deliberate racist legislation, separating families for several generations.
Ukrainian Canadians were unjustly interned during the First World War, in 26 concentrations camps across Canada, yet few Canadians are aware of this.
During World War II, hundreds of Italian Canadians were labelled enemy aliens, separated from families and imprisoned. German Canadians suffered similar injustices.
These injustices would never be tolerated under today's charter of rights. They are shameful events in our history. I call on the Prime Minister to acknowledge each of these injustices against fellow Canadians on behalf of all Canadians.

subtopic: SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
SMALL BUSINESS WEEK
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, during Small Business Week, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the contribution made by small businesses in the riding of Drummond, where leadership and entrepreneurship are a way of life.
As the cornerstone of the Canadian economy, small businesses generate new ideas and are a new source of wealth. Furthermore, they have created nearly three-quarters of the jobs in recent years.
Thanks to the agenda for economic renewal introduced by the Conservative government in 1984, tremendous progress has been made in creating new job opportunities as a result of tax reform, deregulation and the suppression of trade barriers.
Madam Speaker, Canadian entrepreneurs should take advantage of every opportunity they are offered to become even more competitive, innovative and creative, in order to meet the challenges of the 90s.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and in his absence, for the Prime Minister.
October 26, 1990

Yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that Canada was prepared to use force against Iraq, to take part in military action of an offensive nature, without there first being a United Nations resolution approving such action. Today there are reports that the United States is sending another 100,000 troops to the Persian Gulf.
I ask the Prime Minister, is there a pattern here? Is Canada part of a co-ordinated action with the United States to escalate the tensions in the Persian Gulf, and is it doing this without first consulting and getting the approval of our House of Commons?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canada is part of a co-ordinated group of like-minded nations that seek the enforcement of the resolution of the Security Council of the United Nations. We have been part of this group quite properly from the beginning and we would propose to remain there.
What we are doing is enforcing, or seeking the enforcement of, a series of unanimous resolutions, passed by the Security Council of which Canada is a member.
I am quite astonished that the Leader of the Opposition, whose party has supported the general approach of the government, would seek to question it today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the approach that we have supported, and which is stated in the resolution of the House, is in support of United Nations' resolutions condemning Iraqi aggression and the use of sanctions to roll back that aggression.
For weeks now, the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have been telling Canadians that these sanctions are an effective way of rolling back Iraqi aggression against Kuwait and that we must give those sanctions time to work. Yesterday in the House the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs certainly created the impression that Canada had decided that sanctions were not working and was giving up on them.
Why does the government appear to have reached the conclusion that sanctions are not working? What is the evidence for this? Is this conclusion also that of all the other countries which worked to have the resolutions
Oral Questions
adopted at the United Nation to create the system of sanctions to deter and roll back Iraqi aggression?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, obviously everyone in the House knows that the question of the Leader of the Opposition is both a distortion of what the Secretary of State said yesterday and a distortion of the statements of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on behalf of the government over the last two months.
In point of fact, the Secretary of State never said the sanctions are not working, and the Secretary of State did not begin yesterday to point out to members of the House the difficulties inherent in seeking the enforcement of UN resolutions.
Indeed, on October 15, some two weeks ago, the Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote to the spokespeople for external affairs of the Official Opposition parties and said, and I quote: "At the same time, I have also made it clear that if President Hussein does not withdraw from Kuwait, in the face of the unprecedented international consensus and under the pressure of sanctions, he must understand the willingness of the world to take further actions, including military action. Canada is prepared to consider, with its Security Council colleagues, what the next steps might be."
The Secretary of State spelled it out very clearly two weeks ago. I do not know why the Leader of the Opposition expresses the view that this was newly minted information yesterday, when it has been government policy all along.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister quoted the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that Canada would be willing to consider other action with its Security Council colleagues. That can only mean as part of United Nations action.
Yesterday, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said clearly that Canada was ready to take offensive action against Iraq, even though there was no decision first by the United Nations.

In this House yesterday, Madam Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated that the government is considering the possibility of sending our troops

Oral Questions
in offensive action against Iraq, without the approval of the United Nations. That was quite clear, yet the Prime Minister said exactly the contrary when he quoted from a letter of the Secretary of State a few weeks ago.
So I ask the Prime Minister whether he can assure Canadians today that should he decide to involve Canadian troops in offensive action against Iraq, without the sanction of the United Nations, he will not make such a decision without first consulting with and securing the approval of this House?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in addition to the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs which I have just quoted in English, two weeks ago he also advised the opposition as follows: "It stands to reason that in critical times the situation may evolve very rapidly and require immediate action. As you may recall, on September 24 last I said in the House that if there were any change in the gulf situation the government would confer with Parliament." The Leader of the Opposition may claim to be surprised by these statements, but two weeks ago the Secretary of State did say in writing, and I am sure Madam Speaker will allow me to read his statement: "But at the same time I made it quite clear that, if Saddam Hussein does not yield when faced with the unprecedented international consensus which now prevails and with the pressure of sanctions taken against him, he should expect the world community to resort to other measures, including military action. Along with other countries belonging to the Security Council, Canada is prepared to consider what these measures might be."
What the Secretary of State for External Affairs said yesterday was fully consistent with his earlier statements.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question as well for the Prime Minister.
This morning I was in telephone contact with Mrs. Joyce Scobery, whose husband is presently being detained in Iraq, and with Mr. Shiraz Rustom, whose elderly parents are being held against their will in that country. They speak for all those Canadians who have family, loved ones and relatives in Kuwait or Iraq. I want to say to the Prime Minister that they do not understand why the government is not prepared to take special
measures to release their families or loved ones. The present system is not working.
In light of the plea, the request of these families, and in light of the failure so far to gain release of their relatives, will the Prime Minister consent to send a special envoy, a special emissary, a group of parliamentarians, in order to sit down with the Iraqis and negotiate and discuss the release of Canadians who are presently at risk?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, of all of the Canadians who were in Kuwait on August 2, only 3 per cent now remain.
My hon. friend says that he was in conversation this morning with some Canadians. He concluded by saying that they speak for all Canadians held in Iraq.
Last night on The National on the CBC, there were a number of Canadians living in Baghdad interviewed by the CBC. Those who were interviewed said that it would be inappropriate and unacceptable in their judgment for Canada to take action that would diminish the solidarity of the allies in seeking-

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
One was censored who was trying to get out the message that it would be unacceptable to diminish the solidarity of the allies in trying to bring pressure on Saddam Hussein.
My hon. friends may want to examine the transcripts of last night's television program, but those people were certainly speaking in quite a different way from the suggestions of my hon. friend.
What we are ready to do, of course, is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs has repeatedly said. We will examine all options to be helpful to those Canadians who are there. We will seek to do so in a manner that does not diminish the effectiveness or the solidarity of the members of the United Nations Security Council that put together and voted unanimously in favour of a simple, straightforward resolution that calls upon a dictator and an aggressor to withdraw from an innocent country.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Madam Speaker. First, I want to have the Prime Minister confirm that it is true that our present Canadian Ambassador in Iraq has not even had his credentials yet accepted by the Iraqi government

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
One was censored, Brian.

October 26, 1990

and therefore, his ability to undertake direct negotiations is limited.
I would also like him to confirm what the Secretary of State said in the House yesterday, that, in fact, he, the Prime Minister, and President Bush had discussed this question of hostages in Iraq during a telephone conversation one or two days ago. It is clear that success of the emissaries of other countries has been working. It remains a question why we are not doing the same.
Specifically, is the government not undertaking special measures to get Canadians out of Iraq and Kuwait because President Bush asked it not to?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, even my left wing, anti-American friend from Winnipeg knows that that is a completely false suggestion. He knows full well. I will not even dignify that part of what is really a spurious and unacceptable suggestion by a distinguished parliamentarian. I know that, upon reflection, my friend from Winnipeg is going to want to withdraw that kind of suggestion.
The other question was in regard to the effectiveness of the Canadian ambassador whose credentials are questioned by my hon. friend and who was on television last night as well. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister as well.
On August 25, the United Nations passed the resolution supporting an economic blockade against Iraq. The Canadian government sent troops and ships to support that economic blockade.
On Wednesday night, media reports indicated that the blockade was working. On Thursday, the minister responsible for external affairs decided to up the ante, through his inflammatory language, and suggested that Canada would undertake military action without reference to United Nations and without the approval of Parliament. The question that Canadians are asking and that I ask the Prime Minister is this. Is it the policy of the
Oral Questions
Canadian government to undertake unilateral offensive action with the United States without the approval of the UN Security Council?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs discussed the matter in a given context, one of which dimensions implied a possible veto by another or other members of the Security Council.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been deploying his personal efforts and those of his department here and around the world, looking for a peaceful solution to what is a very serious matter. At no time has he "upped the ante", to quote my hon. friend. What he has done is repeated what he conveyed to the spokesperson for External Affairs for my hon. friend's party two weeks ago that there are some very serious consequences that flow from this kind of action and, in a realistic manner, Canada, along with our allies which support the United Nations, must be prepared to envisage those consequences.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, a supplementary to the Prime Minister. I would say to the Prime Minister that the Secretary of State for External Affairs said to the committee that Canada would use force against Iraq, with or without Security Council approval. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the communication that was sent to my hon. friend's party on October 15, the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated very clearly that there would be consultation obviously with the House of Commons. That was very clear cut.
With regard to the statement of yesterday, in its proper context it is fully consistent with the earlier statement set out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Simply put, Canada seeks, along with other members of the Security Council and the 150 members of the United Nations who have endorsed the Security Council position, the respect of the Security Council resolution which calls upon Saddam Hussein to withdraw from Kuwait. It

Oral Questions
is an innocent country that has been a victim of aggression. We hope that the Security Council resolution can be fully implemented.
We are now part of an effort to bring all possible pressure on Saddam Hussein in regard to this, and Canada will maintain that position.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
A supplementary to the Prime Minister. Yesterday, the minister responsible for external affairs said in this House that he would not necessarily ask for Parliament's approval for going to war. He said at page 14692 of Hansard that we cannot always wait, in reference to parliamentary approval.
There is, however, another serious question and that is the question of the hostages in Iraq.

Yesterday's inflammatory statements by the Minister of External Affairs may have some serious consequences for the safety of Canadians being kept hostage in Iraq. Other countries have shown a great deal of prudence and discretion. That is not the case with the Canadian minister who seems to have completely forgotten that the hostages, situation is a precarious one. My question to the Prime Minister is as follows: what does the government intend to do to guarantee the safety of Canadian hostages in Iraq?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the comments made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this respect have been explained at length, not only in a communication from the minister to the hon. member's party on October 15 but also yesterday, in committee, and during Question Period yesterday afternoon. There is no contradiction, none at all, between the position Canada has defended since the beginning of the crisis and the position taken by the Secretary of State yesterday. Only 2 per cent of the Canadians who were in Kuwait on August 2 are still there today. This means that Canada has been very effective in getting Canadian nationals out of the country, does it not?
As for the remaining- Last night, on CBC television, we saw Canadian men and women, including a nurse from Nova Scotia and another Canadian citizen, who seemed to be giving us the message that the Canadian government's policy was appropriate and that they would not approve of sending a special Canadian envoy to
Baghdad to more or less beg the president of Iraq to free Canadian nationals.
As for discretion and prudence, I think that Canada's policy has been not only prudent but effective, ever since the beginning of this crisis. We intend to maintain the same firmness and vigour, and in doing so, we will ask for the co-operation of the hon. member and her party.

Madam Speaker, this is a very important issue for all of us who are members of Parliament from Tbronto. I am happy that the member for Davenport opened the debate today. I know that other members from Toronto are going to be speaking on this debate. I just want to give a short recap of a couple of the points that I made.
As I said before the debate was interrupted for Question Period, there are times when privatization is a good thing and it works. I was not in any way, shape or form casting aspersions on the joint ventures that had built Harbourfront. In fact, I am proud of Harbourfront. As I said earlier, Harbourfront is a multicultural mecca. There is always room for improvement when you are building a large place like that from absolutely nothing. There was a bunch of useless buildings and space which nobody in Toronto had any use for it 10 to 15 years ago. It is now of course a real people place and hundreds of thousands of people enjoy it every week.
The member for Don Valley West said earlier today that there could be a chance that the city of Toronto or the province of Ontario could end up owning Harbourfront. If that were the case, I want to make it perfectly clear that I would have absolutely no problem with that, but this bill does not say that. It is also a very likely possibility that this could go out and whoever in the private sector wants to put the cheque on the table that is determined by this cabinet could walk away with it.
As I said earlier, the taxpayers of Canada have spent about $250 million over many years to put this Harbour-
Govemment Orders
front palace together. It is really not a palace, but it is a place that I am so proud of as a Toronto member that I would hate to think that it is going to go into the hands of someone who does not have the same public purpose. Where else in Canada, or anywhere in North America, have we seen a private sector interest create a public park with the cultural and recreational support facilities such as Harbourfront? I cannot think of anywhere.
There is another thing that concerns me about this bill. It is clause 42. It states:
All obligations and liabilities of Harbourfront Corporation are
deemed to be obligations and liabilities of Her Majesty in the right of
Canada.
I know that there are some contingent liabilities on Harbourfront because of some approvals that were given to developers to advance and build even further density. With just cause, the city has stopped those plans from going forward. There is a contingent liability there for Harbourfront. Let us suppose that we did sell Harbourfront Corporation to a developer for $31 million. My goodness, if the contingent liability, which is the Crown's responsibility, were $30 million, that would mean the possibility exists that we would literally give Harbourfront away.
It is absolutely obscene to put a value of $31 million on Harbourfront. If the government is so convinced that this is a good thing for the people of Canada, if this is a good thing in terms of the public benefit, then let us put all the books and records, and all the deals and linkages on the table. Let us have a full analysis.
I have said this to you before, Madam Speaker. I believe that if the private sector will do the job that is necessary for the public service, let it do that. I support entrepreneurship and I support the private sector. But there are times when it is incumbent upon governments to make sure that they are in a control position to make sure that the public benefit, the public policy objective, is being served. I have seen, and many of us in the House of Commons have seen, time and time again, where the government has sold off things. It sells something that is losing money, and that is a pretty good reason if it can get somebody to come in and do it better. But it even sells things that are doing well.

I am going to give a very specific example and I have mentioned it before. I am absolutely convinced that the privatization of Pearson International Airport is not the right thing to do. Not only that, but the number of people who are involved in this is almost like a monopoly. We cannot have that with a public institution, where it is not optional for the public to use it. We have to use it. I am concerned how this affects tourists coming to the country.
I said this earlier that the profits with Terminals 1 and 2 operating inefficiently were in excess of $70 million last year. Take that over the next 10 years and that is $1 billion that traditionally went into the taxpayers' coffers. You could buy two Terminal 3's for $1 billion, and we, the taxpayers, the Government of Canada, would own them.
What is going to happen when suddenly some of the smaller airports in the country need new services in terms of tarmac, et cetera? We are not going to be in a position to dictate because the public objective is totally different than the private objective. In privatization, it is the absolute right and responsibility to make sure that the private shareholders are served. But in public policy, its the people of Canada who are served.
It is incumbent upon all of us in the House who are accountable to make decisions as to how we govern costs, all the way from the cost of a hamburger in that airport, to a dinner, a rent-a-car, the fees for going to buses, hotels, and everything else. If the private sector controls all of that, then who makes the judgment as to what the public good is all about?
My concern about the disposition of Harbourfront is not because I am in any way, shape or form casting aspersions on the joint ventures of the many good things that have happened at Harbourfront. Some of those joint ventures are actually starting to make a dollar right now. If they can pay back the taxpayer for some of the investment, why would we give it away?
If the province and the city of Toronto so passed it, and this were to go to a private developer, it is not impossible that one developer in the country would control our largest international airport, Pearson, plus our Harbourfront. We cannot be serious about allowing that to happen in a city like this.
If the private sector is convinced that it can do a better job of managing Terminal 1, 2, and 3, let us give them a lucrative management contract. But let us not give away the asset. From year to year, we can judge the management of that. If it is so confident, we can build in incentives and build in bonuses, but we do not need to give away our Harbourfront in Toronto. We do not need to give it away to the private sector so that it have its own private cash boxes.
The government always argues: "Well, where are we going to get the money to build Terminal 3?" If private development can go and get $450 million from the various pension funds and pay a proper rate of interest and it can make a profit on, then so can the government.
Do not compare this to the Dome Stadium or the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto where it is optional whether we use those facilities or not. We must use our airport. We must use our Harbourfront. In no way, shape or form, will I ever support the government giving either of those two things away.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to this horrible piece of legislation. Before I begin to discuss the merits of Bill C-73, again I would like to commend and compliment my friend and colleague from Broadview- Greenwood for his excellent speech that he gave this afternoon, for his continuing concern for the quality of life of people in metropolitan Toronto.
Madam Speaker, here we are on a Friday afternoon in Ottawa talking about something that will have a very direct and negative impact on people in various communities, and I take exception to the strategy employed by the Government of Canada with respect to this piece of legislation.
As you know, Madam Speaker, this legislation was introduced on May 31 of this year. There was no debate in the House at first reading. It was brought back for second reading on Friday, September 28-another Friday. The government, again, is trying to slip through a piece of legislation that it knows is highly unpopular. Here we are again on another Friday afternoon dealing with this bill.
I can tell you, Madam Speaker, whereas some people might have fallen asleep at the switch, the Liberal members in this House have not. In particular, the members from Metropolitan Toronto have not fallen asleep. We know the negative impact of Bill C-73 and we will fight this bill, tooth and nail, here in the House, and at committee, to ensure that Harbourfront in particular is taken care of, that the Government of Canada, or the government of the province of Ontario, or the municipal
October 26, 1990

governments in metropolitan Toronto have control over the assets of Harbourfront and that Harbourfront is not sold to the private sector.
Madam Speaker, as you know, Bill C-73 is a bill that privatizes six Crown corporations which I will list: Canada Harbour Place in Vancouver, B.C., Canada Museums Construction Corporation, the Canadian Livestock Feed Board, the Canadian Patents and Developments Limited, Harbourfront Corporation in the city of Toronto, and Mingan Associates Limited.
This is part and parcel of this government's privatization-crazy mentality. Since the Conservative Party came to office six years ago, it set out in a very systemic and methodical fashion to sell out Canada.
I think it is important at the outset to put this whole matter into perspective. Since 1984, the government has privatized in whole or in part 18 Crown corporations. If we, for a moment, review the track record of this particular government in its attempt to dismantle Canada and in its attempt to sell out Canada, we will see that in fact it is succeeding, given its majority and strategy.
It is slowly but surely succeeding in destroying our country. It is not overkill as far as rhetoric is concerned, because we know that in 1985 one of the first moves of the Conservative government was to eliminate the Foreign Investment Review Agency that gave the Parliament of Canada the legal tools necessary in order to ensure that foreign investment would be to the benefit of Canadians and that there would be a significant benefit to Canada as a result of foreign investment.
Since 1985, it has put up the "for sale" sign. Not only have foreign corporations and foreign capital come to Canada to purchase Canada, of course the government also endorsed and brought in free trade with the United States.
We know now, given the track record of the free trade agreement, that it certainly is not in the best interests of Canada.
What else has it privatized? What other things has this government done to destroy the Canadian dream that we have all cherished and loved over the years? We know that it has attacked the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by severely slashing the budget of the public
Government Orders
broadcaster which has as its main preoccupation the promotion of national unity in Canada.
It is in the process of privatizing Air Canada, the symbol of Canada world-wide. Whenever Canadians travel abroad and see Air Canada or an Air Canada plane, they cannot help but feel proud that there is a piece of Canada. No longer will it be a piece of Canada because of this government's desire to privatize.
Now this government has decided to privatize Petro-Canada, a Crown corporation and oil company in Canada. I believe that Petro-Canada is something that Canadians support in significant numbers.
We know that it has privatized the unemployment insurance program in Canada. It has dismantled VIA Rail. With respect to the airport in Toronto-my friend from Broadview-Greenwood spoke about the situation there-we know that the Government of Canada privatized the construction of Terminal 3. The final chapter has yet to be written with respect to that particular decision of the Government of Canada.
Here we had Pearson International Airport run by the Government of Canada and netting the taxpayers of Canada over $70 million a year, and it decided for whatever reason-presumably one of the reasons was to help its rich developers and business people on Bay Street-to hand over the operation of Terminal 3. Now we know that the government is handing over the operation of Terminals 1 and 2 to the private sector.
The private sector is there for one reason and one reason only; that is, to make a lot of money. As Canadians become aware of what the government is doing to the international airport at Toronto, they are becoming increasingly concerned about the situation there.
The private sector is not there to ensure that Canadians, foreigners and others are able to go to the airport, get onto an airplane and leave on time. The private sector is there to make money for itself, not to help in terms of transportation. It is there to create a shopping centre.
When Terminal 3 opens in several months time, Canadians and Torontonians will see that what was created there is not a structure that will assist in terms of the problems at Pearson International Airport, but it will

October 26, 1990
Government Orders
simply be a huge shopping centre. The goal of the people who will operate Terminal 3 will not be to ensure a transportation system that works efficiently but to ensure that the people stay on the ground for as long as possible in order to spend as much money as possible at the shopping centre that is being built there.
Now we have Bill C-73 that furthers the privatization craziness of the Conservative government. I wish to restrict the remainder of my comments and the remainder of my time to Harbourfront Corporation, which is one of the six Crown corporations that will be privatized as a result of Bill C-73. I would like to put the government on notice today that the Liberal members of Parliament from metropolitan Toronto and other Liberal members of Parliament in the opposition will take a very keen interest and will attack in a very vigorous fashion this piece of legislation because of what it does to Harbourfront.
I work from the premise as a former municipal politician in the city of York in metropolitan Toronto. I see the Minister of State for Housing, a former mayor in the city of East York, is present. We often used to refer to the city of East York in a fond way. We used to call it the city of least York. However, the minister is here and he is the Minister of of State for Housing. Prior to his appointment to cabinet, he was an outspoken critic of issues affecting Torontonians. I know that he is sitting here this afternoon, very concerned about what this government is doing with respect to Harbourfront. I hope that he has spoken out at cabinet against this particular piece of legislation. He will have an opportunity to speak later, and hopefully he will speak for the public record, but I know he agrees that the waterfront in metropolitan Toronto should be a place for people and for parks.
What we have seen over the last number of years, because of the lack of sufficient controls, is the development industry moving into Harbourfront in Toronto and throwing up hotels and luxury condominiums left and right, not for the benefit of Torontonians generally or Canadians generally, but for the benefit of a small group of wealthy people who want to have a condominium on the lake.
I say shame. The lake does not belong to the rich in metropolitan Toronto. The lake belongs to each and every one of us who call Toronto home and to all people who visit Toronto. Toronto is an international city, a city that prides itself in the international community with respect to the amenities it offers to people. We in the metropolitan Toronto caucus of the Liberal Party believe that Harbourfront should be for people.
This particular piece of legislation allows for the privatization of Harbourfront and all the assets of Harbourfront Corporation. Clause 40 (1) of the bill states:
The Minister of Public Works is hereby authorized to procure, on behalf of Her Majesty in right of Canada, the dissolution of Harbourfront Corporation.
Subclause (2) states:
The Minister of Public Works may do all things and perform all acts necessary for or incidental to closing out the affairs of Harbourfront Corporation.
If this bill passes, a big huge for sale sign will be stuck in the sand on the beaches at Harbourfront. The developers like leeches will be swarming to the minister who wants to privatize, making offers not to create a park at Harbourfront, not to create and enhance upon a jewel, as the member referred to it, but to build concrete, to build buildings, to build luxury hotels, to build luxury condominiums. That is wrong because once it is gone, it is gone.
We have certain buildings there, two in particular, the Huang Danczkay condominiums. They are a disgrace to Harbourfront. Those buildings and others are a disgrace to the waterfront. They ought not to have ever been allowed to proceed. Because of the lack of proper controls, we see a situation now where we have a number of very ugly buildings that block the harbourfront in metropolitan Toronto.
When the member for Don Valley West spoke earlier, he said that this bill allows for Harbourfront Corporation to be locally controlled. That is not what it says in this bill. That is not what it says anywhere in this legislation.
This legislation would allow for the sale of Harbourfront Corporation to the highest bidder, to anybody the Minister of Public Works wants to sell to. Once this bill is passed by this Parliament, this Parliament forever and a
October 26, 1990

day will not be able to deal in a direct way with Harbourfront in metropolitan Toronto.
If the member were sincere in what he was saying- and I believe he was-then I am sure that he will support an amendment to this legislation. The Liberal Party intends to move an amendment to ensure that if the Government of Canada no longer wishes to participate and to exercise some degree of control over Harbour-front in metropolitan Toronto, we should hand it over to other government authorities, either to the provincial Government in Ontario, the city of Toronto, to the municipality of metropolitan Toronto, or to a combination of any of the government agencies in metro.
We will not support the sale of the assets of Harbour-front Corporation to the private sector, because we know that the purpose of a sale to the private sector will be to make a lot of money for a very small group of people who will not be here in 50 or 100 years' time. But the waterfront will be here, and we have to ensure that the waterfront in metropolitan Toronto remains a people place. It is a beautiful place for people to gather, especially in the summer months and also in the winter months. We have to ensure that it continues to be a people place, notwithstanding the imperfections that now exist because of the lack of control on the part of different government agencies.
As the member for Broadview-Greenwood said, it is a jewel. It would be a travesty for the remainder of the lands owned by the federal government to be developed in the form of luxury condominiums.
In closing, let me say that we believe strongly that there should continue to be public control over Harbour-front Corporation. We believe that there should be a federal government role in the development of the waterfront because it is a harbour. The government has had for many years a direct role to play with respect to the Toronto harbour.
We look forward to dealing with this bill in a vigorous fashion at committee. I hope this government will come to its senses. It is trying to hoodwink Canadians into believing that the privatization of Harbourfront Corporation is in the best interests of Canadians generally. We do not believe it is. We believe that there ought to have
Government Orders
been more consultation with the people of Toronto. There was not a sufficient amount of consultation.

He said: Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise on this occasion to introduce my private members' bill, Bill C-223, an act respecting a day of mourning for persons killed or injured in the workplace.
Madam Speaker, as you are no doubt aware, this is the second time that I have risen in this House to introduce this legislation. I have been given assurance from representatives of all parties in this House that they will support this legislation and move it forward in order that we may have a law passed by the Parliament of Canada recognizing the contributions that workers across this land have given, and recognizing the fact that many have given their lives.
I am very proud that the Parliament of Canada is moving forward with this legislation. I believe that it is only proper that it be supported by all parties, because all of us know that the issue of health and safety in the workplace is grave and demands immediate action.
I believe that this legislation will go a long way to improving awareness of health and safety issues at a minimal price to the Government of Canada and to employees and employers alike, because we must spend

more time talking about the health and safety of our workers.
This bill calls for the recognition by Parliament and by this nation of April 28 as a national day of mourning for those persons killed or injured in the workplace in Canada. With the number of people who fall victim to workplace injuries, sometimes fatal, it would appear fitting to ask for a week or a month to remember our brothers and sisters. In this legislation, I only ask that the nation remember these people in an official way for one day each year.
Madam Speaker, I ask that we consider the following. In 1987 alone, 1,031,097 persons were injured in the workplace. Of these, 612,886 suffered debilitating injuries, and 887 were reported as fatalities. These figures are staggering and they have remained consistent over the last decade.
Let us not forget those who have died due to exposure to unsafe materials in the workplace. The Public Service Alliance of Canada estimates that between 6,000 to
10,000	Canadian workers each year die as a result of occupational cancer. Yet many of these deaths are not reported as being job related. These people and the dangers they face must be recognized by the Parliament of Canada.
Workers are indeed what make this country productive. It is injuries in the workplace that rob our workers of their health, their lives and their ability to produce. Think of the statistics: every workday, one worker dies each hour; one worker is infirmed each six seconds; one worker is permanently disabled every 12.7 seconds.
Each year, Canada's economy loses 16 million workdays due to workplace accidents, injuries and deaths. To put that into perspective, 16 million workdays are equivalent to all the time and production lost due to strikes and lockouts five times over. It is clear that the issue of health and safety in the workplace is not only a worker's concern, but a concern to all citizens of our nation.
As parliamentarians, it is our duty to look for and find ways to rectify the problems of unsafe working environments. I believe that education and prevention are the best weapons we have to battle the appalling statistics. All employers and workers must recognize the gravity of this issue and become aware of the ways they can improve their odds against injury or death.
Private Members' Business
It is the intent of this legislation to ensure, by recognizing a national day of mourning, that Canadians will institutionalize a day to remember their fellow workers, friends, neighbours and family who were killed or injured while on the job site. This would make workers more aware of the dangers they face, and hopefully help to reverse the alarming trend toward higher and higher casualties. I also believe that a national day giving official recognition would be a catalyst for educational programs and other efforts to use this day at the work site to focus our thoughts and to educate ourselves on the issue of work place safety.
April 28 was the day chosen by the Canadian Labour Congress five years ago as a day for mourning job site casualties, because it was on that day in 1914 that the first worker safety legislation was introduced in a province of Canada. That province was Ontario. We have indeed come a long way since that time in the area of health and safety legislation, but as can be seen by the statistics, there is still much to be done. The passage of this legislation, with the support of members of all parties in the Parliament of Canada, would be a step on the road to a healthy work place in Canada.
As the members will notice, I have introduced an additional clause into Bill C-223 from the legislation I introduced in the past to clarify the status of this day of mourning. This day will not be a legal holiday, and as such, opposition to this legislation cannot be based on the problem of time lost on the job. It is ironic, as I have mentioned, the great loss of time that is caused by work place injury and death, that people would be concerned about the time that would be lost if this was a national holiday.
In order to have this legislation accepted by the House, we have made that amendment to the legislation, and again I thank the members in the other parties for their support.
It is my contention that economic progress cannot be achieved at the expense of health and safety of our workers. I am sure that hon. members will agree with me that we are no longer in the era of the beginning of the industrial revolution. We no longer accept sweat shops. We no longer accept child labour, and we can no longer accept unsafe working conditions for our citizens. We must all take the steps we can to promote safer working environments. We believe that the health and welfare of

our people matters a great deal to all of us. Let us ensure that on April 28 every year, we prove that.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak in support of Bill C-223, an act respecting a day of mourning for persons killed or injured in the workplace. Members will recall that for the past five years, the Minister of Labour has officially acknowledged April 28 as a day of mourning by making a statement in the House and observing a minute of silence in honour of fallen workers and their families.
I believe that by enshrining April 28 in legislation as a day of mourning, it will reinforce in the minds of all of us the terrible losses caused by industrial accidents and diseases. It will also reinforce the need to work constantly and diligently to improve the situation.
In 1988, preliminary figures indicate that more than 800 people died on the job in Canada, and 20 million person days were lost because of work accidents, occupational injuries or illnesses. No one will be unmoved by these figures, I am sure. No loss of life on the job is justifiable, not only from the point of view of the victim's family but also from society's point of view. The direct and indirect costs of work accidents amounted to approximately $22 billion in 1988. That is an enormous burden for our country at any time, but particularly at a time of increasing world competition in trade.
These are telling statistics, but they do not express the tremendous suffering of the accident victims themselves. Often they suffer not only physically but also mentally because they are unable to return to their place of work or earn their living with dignity. These people deserve our help.
We must stand together. We must declare our common determination to fight this terrible scourge, work accidents.
Work conditions and occupational safety and health have evolved greatly since Confederation. At the federal level, there were various pieces of labour-related legislation over the years, but a major step forward was taken in 1968 when the Canada Labour (Safety) Code was adopted.
Occupational safety and health issues are now fundamental to managing the workplace. The rights and duties
of employers and employees are now embedded in our law and regulations. For the federal jurisdiction, the Canada Labour Code is the main vehicle used to further the cause of occupational safety and health.
The code requires that employers make employees aware of all known or foreseeable hazards in the workplace. Workers have the right to refuse dangerous work. Also, workers have the right and responsibility to participate in identifying and solving job-related safety and health problems as members of safety and health committees or as safety and health representatives. Needless to say, they play a key role in further safety and health issues.
We should not become safety conscious only after accidents occur. Prevention has to be foremost in our minds. While laws, regulations, and governments play an important role in accident prevention, in the final analysis it is the employers and the workers who are responsible for preventing, eliminating, or controlling hazards in the workplace. This is a responsibility which no one can shun.
Only through awareness and involvement can Canadian workers significantly improve occupational safety and health in the workplace.
This government favours co-operation and seeking consensus and we are constantly searching for ways to give workers and employers the tools they need to prevent work accidents and occupational injuries and illnesses.
On October, 1988, the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System became operational. This system was created through the joint efforts of federal, provincial and territorial governments, unions, and employers.
The WHMIS is an extremely important system, one of the most advanced of its type in the entire world. Its purpose is to identify and standardize the labelling of hazardous substances used in the workplace. Now that it is operational, this system requires suppliers to state the dangers posed by imported or domestically produced substances that are used in the workplace in Canada. The system also requires suppliers to send data sheets to employers who must then inform their employees of the hazards.

I had the honour and privilege to be briefly our party's labour critic some years ago and that became an area of
special interest to the hon. member and I. We became friends through that. Later I had some satisfaction in a different role here having something to do with allowing our employees to be better able to negotiate with their employer here than they were able to before. As well, in my riding is Lindhurst Hospital which for those involved in rehabilitation therapy is a fairly special place. We see the consequences of work place unhappinesses. I only want to say this.
Today represents one of the things that the present Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland hoped to see some day when he introduced his reform package and that is that we would be able to do more of this in this institution. I want to congratulate the government for accepting a sensible idea and, specifically and importantly, I congratulate the hon. member for Churchill for his initiative. It is because of the possibility of McGrath's reforms and the initiatives of people like the hon. member for Churchill that we will make more progress in this place.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I just have a few short words. I, too, would like to congratulate the hon. member for Churchill for his bill.
As was mentioned by the member from Ottawa, who takes a lot of interest in the workplace, literacy, and numeracy, I also too, have a great interest in all this. It goes all the way back to the child, growing through youth, training, education, and health.
All that leads to less opportunities for accidents in the work place. I think it all ties together. Certainly the minister and the government are pleased to be supportive.
Madam Speaker, you will find that there has been consultation among all parties and that there is agreement to have this bill go to a legislative committee. I suggest that that be put to the House.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, you don't see me rising very often to congratulate a New Democrat but today it is a pleasure to congratulate the hon. member on his excellent initiative.
Before I was elected to Parliament, I became familiar, through my work with the problems that exist in the construction industry. I have worked for engineering firms, and I was involved in the construction industry for 24 years. I saw the safety problems they had on construction sites and I remember the number of deaths that occurred annually, both in the consturction industry and industry in general.
It is therefore a real pleasure today to see that the House is unanimous in its approval, and I hope there will be other times when we will have the same kind of unanimity on other subjects. I say bravo to this excellent initiative, and it is a pleasure to support this bill, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I too would just like to rise and congratulate the member for Churchill before we put the question.
I would just like to mention to the member the significance of what this bill says. If we take a good look at it, it basically says: "A national day of mourning". That is not something to be overly proud of, the fact that we have to have a day to commemorate the death or injury of a lot of Canadians.
I want to bring forward the suggestion of my colleague from Ottawa. Basically this is the starting point of something very significant. It is not out of the question for the government to consider that this should be a national day, a holiday, in one sense; that is, an opportunity for workers all across the country to have the day off work in order to have conferences and to participate in educational endeavours and processes necessary to edu-

cate the public and the workers of just how large an economic and social problem this really is.
I bring that to the member's attention, because it is not pleasant when in this place we have to talk about people's deaths and the reasons why they are occurring in a country that is considered to be one of the most sophisticated and technological in the modem world.
I would like to congratulate the member. I ask members opposite who are in government to consider using this as a starting point, to push it just a little further, and to do what we have done for the environment, for example, which we had once totally ignored. Through initiatives that members made in this place we have carried it to the forefront.
I think the work force and the work place of Canadians is of the utmost importance to us all. We should think very seriously about going forward and not just standing still.
